newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico sugar sector seen dented by corn syrup.
newsitem.headline: Mexico sugar sector seen dented by corn syrup.

text.p: National production and imports of high fructose corn syrup (HFCS) are seen grabbing market share from traditional sugars to supply the Mexican sweetner market, the senior analyst for tropical commodities of Sparks Companies Inc. said here Thursday.

Peter Buzzanell told the F.O. Licht World Sugar and Sweetners' Conference that the direction of Mexico's sugar and HFSC demand in coming years is difficult to forecast but the sweetner of choice in Mexico's large soft drinks industry appears to be in transition toward HFCSs from sugars.

"A transition we are seeing will be hotly contested. One possible outcome by 2001-2002 is an expanded Mexican soft drinks industry requiring 2.1 million tonnes of sweetner, of which Mexican produced sugar supplies nearly one half of the industry's needs or 1 million tonnes," Buzzanell said.

"While domestically produced HFCS provides 450,000 tonnes (21 percent) and imports of HFCS 600,000 tonnes (29 percent)," Buzzanell said. Currently, virtually all sugar is used in the soft drinks industry.

Mexico currently consumes around 1.6 million tonnes of sugar in the soft drinks industry, which is by far the most widely applicable use for HFCSs, with Mexicans only behind the United States in the world in soft drinks consumption per capita.
Buzzanell said Mexicans drink an average 520 eight ounce servings per capita against 828 in the United States.

Among the reasons for the forecast increase in sweetner consumption in soft drinks industry (1.6 million tonnes to 2.1 million tonnes) were Mexico's young population, ongoing problems with potable water and nutrition needs among the poor, Buzzanell said. Soft drinks form a large part of the calorie intake among the lowe echelons of society.
Buzzanell said he expected that in 1997 signs of improvement in the economy suggested growth in the soft drinks industry of up to five percent over 1996.
